successors.name: Himyarite Kingdom
successors.text: Saba's last Cliopatria shape, the Marib country with Najran and the Jawf

ledger.x: c. 800: the Sabaean kingdom at Marib. Saba 'existed in Yemen before 275 CE'; the page (paraphrase) puts its beginning between c. 1000 and c. 800 BCE and cites estimates near 1200, with the heartland at Marib and Sirwah; the History of Yemen page says 'from at least the 11th century BC'. -800 is Cliopatria's first Saba…
7th century: Karib'il Watar conquers the Jawf.
7th century: Najran.

7th century: Hadhramaut under Saba. the Sabaeans page (paraphrase) has Karib'il Watar conquer Awsan, Qataban and Hadhramaut; but the Awsan page has Qataban and Hadhramaut as Saba's 'other allies at the time' of Awsan's fall, and the page itself says that after the 6th century Saba could not…
late 7th century: Saba destroys Awsan.
late 7th century: the Awsan land is divided.
late 7th century: the Awsan land is divided.
6th century: Qataban under Saba.
late 5th century: Qataban is independent again.
383: the north goes to Ma'in.

c. 330: Hadhramaut independent. 'Hadhramaut became independent from Sheba in c. 330 BCE', then allied with the Minaeans and Qataban. The History of Yemen page says 'By the 3rd century BC, Qataban, Hadramout and Ma'in became independent from Saba'.

c. 110 BCE: Saba and Dhu-Raydan. Himyar 'seceded from [Qataban] around 110 BCE and joined Saba to form the kingdom of Saba and Dhu-Raydan'; Cliopatria begins a Himyarite row in -110. The Himyar page has Himyar independent after 110 and conquering Saba c. 25 BCE.
50 BC: Ma'in regained.
26/25 BCE: Rome invades.
25 BCE: the Roman invasion fails.

c. 25 BCE: Himyar conquers Saba. The Himyar page has the kingdom conquer neighbouring Saba (spelled with a final apostrophe there) 'in c. 25 BCE', 'for the first time'. Sabaeans page: 'Greatly economically weakened, the Kingdom of Saba was soon annexed by the Himyarite Kingdom' (no date). Cliopatria keeps a Sabaean…

c. 100: Saba breaks from Himyar. Saba 'freed itself from Himyar by around 100 CE'; the Himyar page has Saba and Qataban 'split from the Kingdom of Ḥimyar' in the early 2nd century AD. Cliopatria's Himyarite shape shrinks in 106 and the Sabaean row returns in 154.

c. 210: Saba and Aksum collide. GDRT of Aksum, 'the first king to be involved in South Arabian affairs', held much of western Yemen (Tihama, Najran, al-Ma'afir, Zafar) and made a pact with the Sabaean king ʿAlhan Nahfan; 'Sabaean and Aksumite interests came into conflict' c. 210-230 under ŠaʿirumYawtar (the…
c. 230: Aksum pushed back. Sabaean pressure Sabaean pressure eventually pushed Aksumite forces back; Aksumite control of Zafar lasts 'until c. 230'.
238: the west and north go to Aksum.
247: the strip returns.

c. 275: Himyar conquers Saba for good. Saba 'was finally permanently conquered by the Himyarites around 275 CE'; Himyar page: 'finally conquered the Sabaean Kingdom around 280', 'By 300, the Himyarite Kingdom had vanquished other political units (including the Saba, Qataban, and Hadrawat kingdoms)'. The History of…
c. 275: the Sabaean kingdom ends (the kingdom 'existed in Yemen before 275 CE'). Cliopatria's Sabaean row runs to 282 and its Himyarite shape widens in 283.

wars.name: Karib'il Watar's campaigns
wars.outcome: Awsan destroyed ('16,000 were killed and 40,000 prisoners were taken') and its land divided between Qataban and Hadhramaut; Nashshan made to pay tribute; the Jawf and Najran taken.

wars.name: Qatabanian-Hadramawt coalition against Saba
wars.outcome: No result recorded: the Qataban page says only that at one point in the 1st century BCE Qataban formed a coalition with Hadramawt, Radman and Madhay against the Sabaeans and gives no details.

wars.name: Aelius Gallus' expedition to Arabia Felix
wars.outcome: A complete failure: the siege was given up and most of the army lost; trade moved to sea routes.

wars.name: Sabaean-Aksumite conflict
wars.outcome: Aksum, which had held much of western Yemen with a Sabaean pact, was pushed back by Sabaean pressure.

certainty.note: All Sabaean frontiers are approximate; no page gives a boundary, and the Gulf of Aden coast and Najran/Jawf extents rest on inscription claims.
